topic: Decoding Wordle: Information Theory and Entropy
target_audience: University students with a basic interest in data science or computer science.

outline.topic: Decoding Wordle: Information Theory and Entropy
outline.target_audience: University students with a basic interest in data science or computer science.

sections.title: Introduction: The Uncertainty Problem
sections.content: Define the challenge of Wordle as a search problem. Introduce 'Uncertainty'—if every word has an equal probability, how do we choose the best one? Connect this to the concept of a 'Decision Tree'.
sections.example: Imagine a detective trying to identify a suspect from a line-up of 64 animals. Each 'Yes/No' question halves the pool.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Measuring Information (The Bit)
sections.content: Explain that information is the reduction of uncertainty. Introduce the formula for Entropy H = -Σ p(x) log2 p(x). Use a visual bar graph showing how a balanced outcome (50/50) provides 1 bit of information.
sections.example: A fair coin flip provides exactly 1 bit of information; a weighted coin (90% Heads) provides very little 'new' information because the outcome is predictable.

sections.title: Applying Entropy to Wordle
sections.content: Explain that a guess in Wordle acts as a partition of the remaining word list. High-entropy guesses are those that split the candidate words into the most evenly-sized groups. Visualize this as a 'branching tree' where each branch has a similar probability weight.
sections.example: Comparing the guess 'ARISE' (which creates many small, balanced sets of outcomes) vs. 'XYLYL' (which creates one huge set and many empty ones).

sections.title: Strategy: Maximizing Expected Information
sections.content: Demonstrate that the optimal guess is the one that maximizes the 'Expected Information Gain'. Show a visual transition where the probability distribution shifts from a flat line (high uncertainty) to a narrow spike (high certainty).
sections.example: A robot choosing between two keys: Key A opens 50 doors, Key B opens 5,000. Key A provides more 'information' about the final target because it narrows the field faster.

sections.title: Conclusion: Beyond Luck
sections.content: Summarize that 'optimal' play is simply the mathematical reduction of entropy. Final takeaway: Information theory transforms a game of intuition into a predictable computational process.
sections.example: The 'Wordle Bot' uses this exact logic: calculating the entropy of every possible word against the remaining dictionary to make the next move.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Uncertainty Problem
lecture_lines: Wordle is essentially a challenging search problem.
Uncertainty arises when all words seem equally probable.
We use decision trees to narrow the search.
Each guess helps us halve the candidate pool.
Information theory guides us to the best guess.

storyboard.title: Applying Entropy to Wordle
lecture_lines: Every guess partitions the remaining word list.
High-entropy guesses create more balanced outcomes.
Visualizing as a branching tree helps.
Good guesses split candidates into similar sizes.
Bad guesses leave one huge remaining set.

lecture_lines: Optimal guesses maximize expected information gain.

Higher certainty means fewer remaining possibilities.

Logic replaces intuition in this game.
